title: Autumn Leaves & Conkers
strapline: Crunch through the leaves, fill your pockets with conkers, and watch the whole world turn gold and brown.
intent: Autumn hands children a season they can hear, smell and feel — the crunch underfoot, the smell of damp leaves, the cold shine of a fresh conker — and provision that catches that gives their curiosity somewhere real to go.
Gathering, sorting and comparing leaves and conkers is early mathematics that needs no worksheet: big and small, smooth and prickly, most and fewest.
The changing tree is a first, memorable lesson in seasons and time — leaves that were green in September are red and falling now, and children begin to expect the pattern.
Handling small, precious natural things builds fine-motor control and the deep satisfaction of a collection that is entirely one's own.
Autumn pours in language — golden, crunchy, conker, acorn, bare, falling — words rooted in something the child has just held.
Being out among the changing trees grows a genuine care for the living world and the seasons that turn it.
implementation: Get outside while it's happening — a leaf-kicking walk, a conker hunt under the tree, bags and baskets for the treasures children choose to keep.
Bring the haul back to a low table with magnifiers, sorting trays and hoops, and sit alongside wondering aloud: 'I wonder which leaf is the biggest — how could we find out?'
Model the noticing talk: 'This one's gone crispy and brown, but this one's still a bit green — why do you think that is?'
Weave in maths as you play: count the conkers into egg boxes, sort leaves by colour or size, line them up longest to shortest.
Offer real jobs — a leaf pile to jump in and rake, conkers to thread, acorns to post into tubes — and let children set their own challenges.
Keep it going across the weeks: revisit the same tree, photograph how it changes, and let the collection grow bare as the branches do.
key_questions: Which leaf is the biggest — how could we find out?
Why do you think this one has gone brown but that one is still green?
Can you sort these into the smooth ones and the prickly ones?
How many conkers have you collected? Shall we count them into the egg box?
What do you think this tree will look like next time we come?

impact.text: Children sort and group leaves and conkers by their own rule — colour, size, smooth or prickly — and can tell you the rule.
Children count their collection and compare amounts and sizes — biggest, smallest, most, fewest.
Children notice the weather and season and what it means, watching the same tree change over the weeks.
Children handle small natural treasures with care and thread, post and collect them with growing control.
Children pick up and use new autumn words — golden, crunchy, conker, acorn, bare — rooted in what they have just held.

enhancements: A rolling autumn treasure table by the window that grows fuller through the season and is pored over all week.
Conker threading and acorn-posting into cardboard tubes for fine-motor work with the day's finds.
Leaf printing and bark rubbings, then sorting the prints biggest to smallest.
A 'my tree' visit to the same tree each week, photographing how bare the branches become.
A note home inviting families to send a leaf or conker from a weekend walk.

playing_exploring: Children gather and handle real autumn treasures, following their own fascination with what to keep and what to compare.
Every sense is drawn in — the crunch, the smell, the cold smooth conker turned over in the hand.
active_learning: Children return to the same tree and collection over the weeks, staying with the slow story of the season.
creating_thinking: Children invent their own ways to sort and order the leaves, and notice patterns of change from one visit to the next.
